summary: This RFC identifies the documents specifying the official protocols used in the Internet and obsoletes RFC 924 and earlier editions. It is an official status report on the protocols in the ARPA Internet community and was replaced by RFC 961.

plainLanguage.summary: A refreshed list of the official network rulebooks for the year. Another newer list replaced it.

questions: what were the official arpa internet protocols in 1985
what is the difference between required recommended and experimental protocols
subtitle: The 1985 update to the official Internet protocols catalog.

tldr.problem: Internet protocol development was evolving rapidly, and the community needed an updated official list reflecting the latest standards.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC updates and replaces RFC 924 with the current status of all official protocols, noting recent changes and improvements.
tldr.outcome: It served as the authoritative protocol list for April 1985 but was itself superseded by RFC 961 later that year as the protocol suite continued to mature.

today: RFC 944 is Historic. It was superseded by RFC 961 in June 1985, continuing the rapid evolution of Internet protocol standards as the ARPA-Internet grew.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 944 identifies the documents specifying the official protocols used in the Internet and is an official status report for the ARPA-Internet community. It obsoletes RFC 924 and earlier editions and reflects updates made to the protocol suite in the first months of 1985.

The RFC notes that official protocols primarily come from the "Internet Protocol Transition Workbook" (IPTW) dated March 1982. Revised protocol families have been issued in specialized volumes including "Internet Mail Protocols," "Internet Telnet Protocol and Options," and the "Internet Protocol Implementers Guide."
sections.plainLanguage: This is the official list of network rules the Internet follows in 1985. It replaces the 1984 list and includes updates about what is working well and what needs fixing.

sections.title: Organization and Status Categorization
sections.content:
The RFC organizes protocols by functional level (overview, network level, host level, and application level) with consistent information for each protocol. Every entry includes:

  • STATUS: the implementation requirement (required, recommended, elective, or experimental)
  • SPECIFICATION: the document defining the protocol
  • COMMENTS: notes on differences, issues, or planned changes
  • OTHER REFERENCES: related documents and implementations
  • DEPENDENCIES: which other protocols this protocol requires
  • CONTACT: a person who can answer technical questions

The status categories indicate how broadly protocols should be implemented across Internet hosts and gateways.
sections.plainLanguage: Every protocol is described the same way: what status it has, which document defines it, what problems people found, and who to ask about it.

sections.title: Network Infrastructure Protocols
sections.content:
Internet Protocol (IP), specified in RFC 791, is required and forms the universal foundation of the Internet. It provides datagram delivery with addressing for all hosts. The RFC notes ongoing work on IP security options and confirms that ICMP is an integral part of IP implementation.

Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP), specified in RFC 792, is required. It carries control messages and error reports for IP. RFC 944 notes that additional ICMP message types for address information exchange are under experimental development, with details still subject to change.

Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) is recommended for gateways to exchange routing information between different administrations. Gateway Gateway Protocol (GGP) remains experimental and is used in core Internet gateways. References to external networking standards like MIL-STD-1777 (military IP standard) are included.
sections.plainLanguage: IP is the backbone rule that moves data between all computers. ICMP tells computers when problems happen. Gateway protocols help the Internet's traffic routers communicate.

sections.title: Host Transport and Application Protocols
sections.content:
User Datagram Protocol (UDP), specified in RFC 768, is recommended. It adds port-based addressing on top of IP for fast message delivery without guaranteed delivery. Transmission Control Protocol (TCP), specified in RFC 793, is recommended. It provides reliable, ordered streams of data and is widely used for applications requiring data integrity.

The RFC includes extensive comments on TCP implementation issues, including window acknowledgement strategy (RFC 813), address and port conventions (RFC 814), fault handling, and segment size parameters. It also notes experimental protocols like Stream Protocol (ST) for real-time resource allocation and Host Monitoring Protocol (HMP) for remote system debugging.

Telnet Protocol, specified in RFC 854, is recommended for interactive remote terminal access. Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) and mail protocols are covered in the "Internet Mail Protocols" volume. The RFC references the comprehensive Telnet Options list and other specialized protocols for different application needs.
sections.plainLanguage: UDP is the fast, simple way to send messages without guarantees. TCP is the reliable way to send complete messages that must arrive in order. Telnet lets you use a distant computer, and other protocols handle email and specialized services.

sections.title: Experimental and Emerging Protocols
sections.content:
The RFC documents several experimental protocols still under development. Network Voice Protocol (NVP-II) defines procedures for real-time voice conferencing over the Internet. Reliable Data Protocol (RDP) is designed for bulk data transfer in high-delay or high-loss environments, useful for remote monitoring and debugging.

Multiplexing Protocol (MUX) combines segments from multiple higher-level protocols into one IP datagram. Internet Reliable Transaction Protocol (IRTP) provides a transport-level protocol for host-to-host communication in Internet environments.

The RFC emphasizes the need to coordinate with protocol contacts before implementation of experimental protocols to ensure proper testing and integration with the broader Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: New protocols are being tested for voice, for moving large files reliably, for combining multiple messages, and for special transaction handling. These are not yet official but may become part of the standard suite.
